title: Nervous shock is a historical label for actionable psychiatric injury caused by wrongful conduct

content.overview: Nervous shock is a historical label for actionable psychiatric injury caused by wrongful conduct. Modern analysis proceeds through negligence and distinguishes primary victims directly endangered from secondary victims witnessing harm to another.
content.glance: Nervous shock is a historical label for actionable psychiatric injury caused by wrongful conduct. Modern analysis proceeds through negligence and distinguishes primary victims directly endangered from secondary victims witnessing harm to another.
content.study: Nervous shock is a historical label for actionable psychiatric injury caused by wrongful conduct. Modern analysis proceeds through negligence and distinguishes primary victims directly endangered from secondary victims witnessing harm to another.\n\nThe common law moved toward recognition of medically established psychiatric injury. McLoughlin v O'Brian and Alcock refined proximity requirements for secondary victims. The claimant must distinguish recognised psychiatric illness from ordinary grief or distress.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective & Doctrinal Foundations
sections.body: The common law moved toward recognition of medically established psychiatric injury. McLoughlin v O'Brian and Alcock refined proximity requirements for secondary victims. The claimant must distinguish recognised psychiatric illness from ordinary grief or distress.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Provisos & Statutory Deconstruction
sections.body: The claim is not established by emotional upset alone. Duty, breach, causation and recognised psychiatric injury are required, with stricter proximity controls for secondary victims.

sections.heading: Mandatory Proving Ingredients & Essential Elements
sections.body: 1. Recognised psychiatric injury. 2. Duty and breach. 3. Factual and legal causation. 4. Foreseeability. 5. For secondary victims, qualifying relationship, proximity and direct perception as required by precedent.

sections.heading: Evidentiary Burdens under BSA 2023 (ss. 104–106 & s. 63)
sections.body: Medical evidence is central. Relationship to the primary victim, location, timing and manner of perception may determine proximity. Ordinary distress without recognised psychiatric illness is not automatically actionable.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Competent Forum & Limitation Act Checkpoints
sections.body: Plead the duty, breach, psychiatric injury and causation. Expert evidence may be required. Limitation depends on the applicable personal-injury regime and facts.

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Doctrine Satisfied
examples.body: Secondary-victim claims are controlled by proximity requirements; primary victims face a different duty analysis. The claimant must still prove the remaining ingredients on the civil standard.

examples.title: Illustration 2 — Boundary Defect
examples.body: Actionable psychiatric injury ordinarily requires a recognised psychiatric illness, not ordinary grief or distress. A court should not infer liability from the label alone.

cases.name: McLoughlin v O'Brian
cases.facts: Secondary-victim claims are controlled by proximity requirements; primary victims face a different duty analysis.
cases.issue: What legal rule governs the doctrine?
cases.ratioDecidendi: A secondary victim may recover for a recognised psychiatric injury after seeing injured family in the immediate aftermath. Proximity of relationship, time and space, and direct perception control the claim. Citation already in this file: [1983] 1 AC 410.
cases.holding: Secondary-victim claims are controlled by proximity requirements; primary victims face a different duty analysis.
cases.relevance: Use the case for its stated ratio and apply it to the proved facts.

cases.name: Alcock v Chief Constable of South Yorkshire Police
cases.facts: Secondary-victim claims are controlled by proximity requirements; primary victims face a different duty analysis.
cases.issue: What legal rule governs the doctrine?
cases.ratioDecidendi: Secondary-victim claims from Hillsborough were dismissed. The claimant needs a close tie of love and affection, proximity to the event or its immediate aftermath, and perception through the claimant's own senses. Citation already in this file: [1992] 1 AC 310.
cases.holding: Secondary-victim claims are controlled by proximity requirements; primary victims face a different duty analysis.
cases.relevance: Use the authority for the precise proposition it decides.
